title: What happened
goal: Tell what happened — where you went, what you did, saw and said — using the simple past, including Sindhi's 'ergative' past of transitive verbs and pronoun endings on verbs.
intro:
The Sindhi past tense comes in two flavours. With verbs **without an object** (go, come, sleep) it works like the present: the verb agrees with the subject — **هو آيو** 'he came', **هوءَ آئي** 'she came'.

With verbs **that take an object** (eat, see, say, do), Sindhi switches perspective: the doer goes into the **oblique** form and the verb agrees with the **object**: **مون ماني کاڌي** 'I ate food' — literally 'by me, food (f) was eaten'. This is the famous **ergative** pattern of Indo-Aryan languages. Unlike Urdu, Sindhi has **no ergative marker** (no نے) — the oblique pronoun is enough.

And Sindhi has one more trick: the doer can be **attached to the verb** as an ending — **ڏٺم** 'I saw', **چيائين** 'he/she said'.

grammar.title: The past of intransitive verbs (agreeing with the subject)
grammar.body:
Verbs without an object form the past with a **participle** that agrees with the subject like an adjective: **-o** (m sg), **-ī** (f sg), **-ā** (m pl), **-yūṃ** (f pl):

اچڻ → آيو āyo / آئي āī / آيا āyā / آيون āyūṃ — came
وڃڻ → ويو vayo / وئي vaī / ويا vayā / ويون vayūṃ — went (irregular)
ٿيڻ → ٿيو thiyo / ٿي thī / ٿيا / ٿيون — became, happened
سمهڻ → سمهيو sumhyo — slept; اٿڻ → اٿيو uthyo — got up; پهچڻ → پهتو pahuto — arrived (irregular); نڪرڻ → نڪتو nikto — left (irregular).

For **I** and **we** Sindhi adds person endings: **مان آيس** āyus (man) / **آئيس** āīs (woman) 'I came'; **مان ويس** viyus / **وئيس** vaīs 'I went'; **اسين آياسين** āyāsīṃ 'we came', **وياسين** vayāsīṃ 'we went'. (For 'you' and 'they', the bare participle is normal in speech: توهان آيا 'you came', هو ويا 'they went'.)

**Was**: هو ho / هئي huī / هئا huā / هيون huyūṃ; 'I was' هوس hos (m) / هيس huyas (f).

examples.en: The train arrived on time. (ٽرين f)

examples.roman: māṃ guzriyala sāla lanḍan meṃ hos.
examples.en: I was in London last year. (man)

grammar.title: The past of transitive verbs: the ergative construction
grammar.body:
When a verb has an **object**, the past works differently:

1. The **doer** goes into the **oblique** form — but with **no extra marker** (Urdu adds نے; Sindhi doesn't): مون 'by me', تو 'by you (intimate)', هن 'by him/her', اسان 'by us', توهان 'by you (polite)', هنن 'by them'; nouns take their oblique: ڇوڪري (boy, chhokire), علي.
2. The **verb agrees with the object**, not the doer: مون **ڪتاب** پڙهيو (ڪتاب m → -o), مون **چٺي** پڙهي (چٺي f → -ī), مون **ڪتاب** پڙهيا (m pl → -ā).

So 'I ate' depends on what you ate: مون انب کاڌو (mango, m) vs مون ماني کاڌي (bread, f). If there's no visible object, or the object is a whole clause, use the default **masculine singular**: هن چيو ته … 'he/she said that …'.

Common irregular past participles: ڪرڻ → **ڪيو** kayo · کائڻ → **کاڌو** khādho · پيئڻ → **پيتو** pīto · ڏسڻ → **ڏٺو** ɗiṭho · چوڻ → **چيو** chayo · ڏيڻ → **ڏنو** ɗino · وٺڻ → **ورتو** varto · ٻڌڻ → **ٻڌو** ɓudho.

examples.en: I bought an ajrak. (اجرڪ f → ڪئي)
The boy wrote a letter. (ڇوڪري = chhokire, oblique of ڇوڪرو)
Did you hear what I said? (lit. my words, f pl)

grammar.title: Pronoun endings on verbs: ڏٺم 'I saw', چيائين 'he said'
grammar.body:
In everyday Sindhi — and constantly in stories — the doer of a transitive past verb is often **attached to the verb as a suffix** instead of being said as a separate word:

**-m / -um** = by me: ڏٺم ɗiṭhum 'I saw', چيم chayum 'I said', ڪيم kayum 'I did', کاڌم khādhum 'I ate'
**-āīṃ** = by him/her: ڏٺائين ɗiṭhāīṃ 'he/she saw', چيائين chayāīṃ 'he/she said', ڏنائين ɗināīṃ 'he/she gave', ڪيائين kayāīṃ 'he/she did'
**-āūṃ** = by them: چيائون chayāūṃ 'they said', ڪيائون kayāūṃ 'they did'
**-sīṃ** = by us: ڪيوسين kayosīṃ 'we did', ڏٺوسين ɗiṭhosīṃ 'we saw'

The verb still agrees with the object underneath, so the stem can change: ماني کاڌيم khādhīm 'I ate the bread (f)'. You can always use the full form (مون ڏٺو، هن چيو) — but you must **recognise** these endings, because Sindhi speakers use them all the time.

examples.en: I saw a lovely film yesterday. (فلم f → ڏٺيم, pronounced ɗiṭhīm)

examples.native: هن کان پڇيم، پر ڪجهه نه چيائين.
examples.roman: hun khāṃ puchhyum, para kujhu na chayāīṃ.
examples.en: I asked him, but he didn't say anything.

examples.native: اسين سڄو ڏينهن گهمياسين، پوءِ ماني کاڌيسين.
examples.roman: asīṃ saʄo ɗīṃhu ghumyāsīṃ, poi mānī khādhīsīṃ.
examples.en: We wandered all day, then we ate. (intransitive گهمياسين vs transitive suffixed کاڌيسين)

dialogue.title: A trip to Mohenjo-daro
dialogue.setting: On Monday morning, Marvi asks her colleague John about his weekend.

lines.speaker: Marvi
lines.native: جان، موڪل ڪيئن گذري؟ ڇا ڪيو؟
lines.roman: Jān, mokala kīeṃ guzrī? chhā kayo?
lines.en: John, how was the weekend? What did you do?

lines.speaker: John
lines.en: Sarah and I went to Larkana.

lines.speaker: John
lines.native: ها! ڇنڇر تي صبح جو سوير نڪتاسين ۽ ڏهين وڳي پهتاسين.
lines.roman: hā! chhanchhara te subuh jo sver niktāsīṃ ai ɗahīṃ vaɠe pahutāsīṃ.
lines.en: Yes! On Saturday we set off at dawn and arrived at ten.

lines.speaker: John
lines.native: اسان سڄو شهر گهميو — گهٽيون، کوهه، وڏو حمام.
lines.roman: asāṃ saʄo shaharu ghumyo — ghiṭyūṃ, khūha, vaɗo hamāmu.
lines.en: We walked around the whole city — the streets, the wells, the Great Bath.

lines.speaker: John
lines.native: ڏاڍي هئي! سارا ته پاڻيءَ جون پنج بوتلون پيتيون.
lines.roman: ɗāḍhī huī! Sārā ta pāṇīa jūṃ panja botalūṃ pītyūṃ.
lines.en: Very! Sarah drank five bottles of water.

lines.speaker: Marvi
lines.en: What did the guide tell you?

lines.speaker: John
lines.native: چيائين ته هي شهر پنج هزار سال پراڻو آهي.
lines.roman: chayāīṃ ta hī shaharu panja hazāra sāla purāṇo āhe.
lines.en: He said this city is five thousand years old.

lines.speaker: John
lines.native: رستي ۾ سنڌي برياني کاڌيسين ۽ رات جو دير سان موٽياسين.
lines.roman: raste meṃ sindhī biryānī khādhīsīṃ ai rāti jo dera sāṃ moṭyāsīṃ.
lines.en: We had Sindhi biryani on the way and got back late at night.

culture: **Mohenjo-daro** (موهن جو دڙو, 'mound of the dead'), near Larkana, was one of the great cities of the Indus Valley Civilisation, flourishing around 2500 BCE with planned streets, brick houses, drains and the famous Great Bath. It is a UNESCO World Heritage Site and a source of deep pride in Sindh, which sees itself as heir to one of humanity's first urban cultures. Sindh's later history includes the Arab conquest of 711–712 CE, the Soomra and Samma dynasties (whose capital at Thatta left the vast Makli necropolis), the Kalhora and Talpur rulers, and British annexation in 1843.

tip.title: Came, went, left: the past of "go"-type verbs
tip.body:
- Verbs with no object agree with the **subject** like an adjective: آيو (m) · **آئي** (f) · **آيا** (pl) 'came'; ويو · وئي · ويا 'went'.
- For 'I' and 'we' add an ending: مان **ويس** / **وئيس** 'I went' (man / woman), اسين **وياسين** 'we went'.
- Irregular: پهچڻ → **پهتو**, نڪرڻ → **نڪتو**.
tip.pattern: هو آيو · هوءَ آئي · مان آيس · اسين آياسين

lessons.title: It was, they were: the old days

tip.title: Was and were
tip.body:
- 'Was' agrees too: **هو** (m) · **هئي** (f) · **هئا** (m pl); 'I was' = **هوس** (man) / **هيس** (woman).
- 'Was born' = **ڄائو** (m) / **ڄائي** (f): هو ڳوٺ ۾ ڄائو.
- 'Died' is intransitive: **مري ويو / مري وئي** (politely: گذاري ويو).

lessons.title: What did you eat, see and say?

tip.title: مون ماني کاڌي — "by me, bread was eaten"
tip.body:
- With an object, the doer takes the oblique form: **مون** (I), **هن** (he/she), **اسان** (we), توهان (you) — no extra word like Urdu نے.
- The verb agrees with the **object**: مون انب **کاڌو** (m) · مون ماني **کاڌي** (f) · مون ڪتاب **ورتا** (pl).
- No object? Use the masculine: هن **چيو** ته …
tip.pattern: مون / هن / اسان + object + verb (agrees with object)

new: هن مون کي ڪجهه به نه ٻڌايو.

tip.title: I lost it / it got lost
tip.body:
- 'I lost X' has an object, so the verb agrees with X: مون ڪنجي **وڃائي** (f), مون پئسا **وڃايا** (pl).
- 'X got lost' has no object: ڪنجي **گم ٿي وئي**، فون **گم ٿي ويو**.
- 'X won't turn up' = X **نٿو لڀي**.

sentences.native: مون هن جو نالو وساري ڇڏيو.
sentences.roman: moṃ hun jo nālo visārī chhaɗyo.
kālha bāzāra meṃ hiku vāqiʿo thiyo.
sentences.en: Something happened in the bazaar yesterday.

tip.title: The doer as an ending
tip.body:
- In speech the doer is often stuck onto the past verb: **-m** 'by me' (ڏٺم 'I saw'), **-āīṃ** 'by him/her' (چيائين 'he/she said'), **-āūṃ** 'by them' (ڪيائون 'they did').
- It means the same as مون ڏٺو، هن چيو، هنن ڪيو.
- 'Start' has two verbs: شروع **ڪرڻ** (you start something) and شروع **ٿيڻ** (it starts).

sentences.en: I asked him, but he didn't tell me anything.
